entries.note:
The first version bound an ephemeral port per worker, which looked obviously right and was obviously wrong the first time a layered update ran: the port moved from 49953 to 61709 and the owner's own connected session reported `WebSocket connection to 'ws://127.0.0.1:49953/' failed`. Claude Code reads a lock once, then reconnects to the port it read; it does not go back to the directory to look again. So an IDE whose port moves is an IDE that dies on every update — in a feature whose entire premise is that capabilities arrive *by* update (KI-066).

The port therefore belongs to the runtime, not to the worker: the supervisor reserves it once and hands the same number to every worker it starts. A worker starting during an update finds its predecessor still holding it, because the successor is started before the old one retires, so it retries for a bounded while instead of taking a free port. Taking a free port is the tempting fallback and it is the bug: it succeeds, logs nothing, and silently ends every session. Failing to get the port leaves the bridge unpublished with a reason, which someone can see.

The loop checks `closed` after every sleep and never before a bind: a successor retired while waiting must not take the port after its own retirement and publish a lock nobody will unlink. That rule had no case until a sabotage that ignored `closed` passed the record — the retirement merely took longer — so the case closes the successor and its predecessor concurrently, where the difference is a lock on disk.

entries.note:
The lock carries an `authToken` and the CLI's binary never says where it presents it. The first implementation accepted it in any of three plausible places — header, query string, subprotocol — which is the kind of hedge that survives forever because nothing ever disproves it. Driving the real CLI settled it instead: `claude` 2.1.263 connects with `x-claude-code-ide-authorization: <token>` and asks for the `mcp` subprotocol (headers recorded in the evidence document). The hedge was then deleted. If a future version moves the token, this refuses the connection and the handshake fails loudly, which is the intended outcome: the alternative is a socket that accepts whatever a local process offers.

The comparison is on the header value as HTTP delivers it — trailing whitespace already trimmed, a duplicated header joined with `, ` the way Node joins one — and the record holds both: a token followed by a space is accepted, a token presented twice is not.

Ported from `orchestrator/runtime/ide.mjs` (spec 129); the JavaScript this describes is gone.

The SDK answered every request on its own promise, so a `ping` sent behind a slow `getDiagnostics` was answered first; the diagnostics source is the language servers, reached over a pipe and then a socket, and a read loop that awaited it would hold every later frame from that CLI behind it. Only the diagnostics call is spawned: everything else is answered inline, in order, because a multi-thread runtime would otherwise be free to answer two synchronous requests out of the order they arrived in, which the single-threaded SDK never did.
